lines.text: In the Second World War, the Polish army enlisted a bear.
He had a rank, a serial number, and a taste for beer.
In 1942, Polish soldiers in Iran adopted an orphaned bear cub.
lines.say: In nineteen forty-two, Polish soldiers in Iran adopted an orphaned bear cub.

lines.text: They fed him condensed milk from an old vodka bottle, and named him Wojtek.
lines.say: They fed him condensed milk from an old vodka bottle, and named him Voy-tek.

lines.text: He grew up copying the soldiers. He wrestled them, saluted, and marched on his hind legs.
Then the army sailed for Italy, and the ship did not allow pets.
So the soldiers made him one of them: Private Wojtek, with his own paybook.
lines.say: So the soldiers made him one of them: Private Voy-tek, with his own paybook.

lines.text: In 1944, at the battle of Monte Cassino, his unit says he carried crates of artillery shells, and never dropped one.
lines.say: In nineteen forty-four, at the battle of Monte Cassino, his unit says he carried crates of artillery shells, and never dropped one.

lines.text: He was promoted to corporal, and a bear carrying a shell became the company badge.
After the war, he retired to Edinburgh Zoo, where old soldiers came to visit.
He still answered when they spoke to him in Polish.
